summary:
S.E.L.E.N.E. Ops is an interactive platform for finding and evaluating Earth analog sites for future Moon-base and Mars missions. Discovery ranks candidate terrain against specific lunar and Martian targets using measured elevation geometry, while Scout lets users draw a search zone and investigate promising micro-sites. Mission Control compares Earth and planetary terrain in 3D, explores environmental processes, and runs simulated landing and rover rehearsals. A route explorer maps regional slopes, relief, modeled shadows, and Sentinel-1 radar context to guide further investigation.

Every result identifies its sources, scale, and limitations. Its geometric index measures terrain characteristics, not overall planetary similarity. By connecting open NASA and partner-agency data to practical mission questions, S.E.L.E.N.E. Ops helps teams prioritize where to test equipment and methods—and understand where each Earth analogy breaks down—before exploring the Moon or Mars.
details:
S.E.L.E.N.E. Ops (Surface Exploration, Lithology & Environment Network Engine) helps teams identify and investigate Earth locations that could support Moon and Mars exploration tests. It combines a catalog of documented analog sites with four Earth–planetary reference scenarios. Discovery searches for new candidates using terrain and climate context; Scout lets users draw a search area and rank smaller sites within it.

The application compares Earth terrain with lunar and Martian elevation products using slope, relief, and terrain roughness measures. Its index describes selected geometric characteristics, not overall planetary similarity. Mission Control presents the paired landscapes in 3D and supports simulated landing and rover rehearsals. A route explorer examines regional slopes, relief, modeled shadows, and Sentinel-1 radar context. Published evidence for the Marius Hills pit and La Corona lava tube adds a limited subsurface comparison. Users can export findings with source, resolution, coverage, and limitations attached.

The intended benefit is to help researchers and exploration teams prioritize field sites and test plans while seeing where an Earth analogy breaks down. Routes are investigation hypotheses, not certified safe traverses; the rover and landing sequences are simulations.

We built the browser interface with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js, and WebGL; the backend uses Python and FastAPI. Geospatial processing uses STAC catalogs and Python raster libraries. The project runs on an ordinary computer and requires no custom hardware. Its creative contribution is the connected workflow from broad discovery to local analysis, mission rehearsal, and traceable evidence, with missing data shown explicitly rather than filled with invented measurements.
